2020-Q1.shortcut: Under U(0,2), F0(x) = x/2. Sort the data (0.08, 0.16, 0.16, 0.32, 0.98) and compare the step function with F0; the largest gap occurs just after x = 0.32, where Fn = 0.8 and F0 = 0.16, giving D = 0.64.
tips: Always evaluate the gap on BOTH sides of each jump: |i/n - F0(x_i)| and |(i-1)/n - F0(x_i)|. The maximum of all these is D.
Handle the tie at 0.16 by jumping the empirical CDF straight from 0.2 to 0.6 - two observations share the point, so the step has height 2/5.
The uniform CDF on (0,2) is x/2, so the theoretical values 0.04, 0.08, 0.08, 0.16, 0.49 are trivial to write down; most of the work is bookkeeping, not arithmetic.
The data are heavily concentrated near 0 while U(0,2) spreads to 2, so a LARGE D is expected - options (a) 0.16 and (b) 0.52 understate the mismatch.
solution: Under H0 the distribution is U(0,2), so F0(x) = x/2 for 0 <= x <= 2.
The empirical CDF takes the values 0.2 after 0.08, 0.6 after the tied pair at 0.16, 0.8 after 0.32 and 1.0 after 0.98.
Compute the deviations at each point (both before and after the jump): at 0.08, |0.2 - 0.04| = 0.16; at 0.16, |0.6 - 0.08| = 0.52; at 0.32, |0.8 - 0.16| = 0.64; at 0.98, |1.0 - 0.49| = 0.51.
The pre-jump deviations (0.04, 0.12, 0.44, 0.31) are all smaller.
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is the largest of these, D = 0.64, option (c).

2020-Q2.shortcut: Row sums give X1 + X2 = 100 and Y = 18. Equal column totals for C and D give X1 + 46 = X2 + 78, i.e. X1 - X2 = 32. Solving, X1 = 66 and X2 = 34.
tips: Extract every equation the table offers BEFORE solving: each row total is one equation and the stated condition is another. Three unknowns need three equations.
The 'not leaked' row is fully determined except for Y, so Y = 400 - (90 + 46 + 78 + 168) = 18 comes out immediately and independently.
Sum and difference: X1 + X2 = 100 and X1 - X2 = 32 give X1 = 66 and X2 = 34 by inspection - add and halve.
Options (a) and (b) differ only by swapping X1 and X2, so pin down which column is C: the larger leaked count goes with the SMALLER not-leaked count (46) to keep the totals equal.
solution: From the 'not leaked' row: 90 + Y + 46 + 78 + 168 = 400, so Y = 400 - 382 = 18.
The column total for material C is X1 + 46 and for material D is X2 + 78; these are stated to be equal.
Hence X1 + 46 = X2 + 78, giving X1 - X2 = 32.
Solving X1 + X2 = 100 with X1 - X2 = 32: X1 = 66 and X2 = 34.
Check: column C total = 66 + 46 = 112 and column D total = 34 + 78 = 112, equal as required. Option (a) is correct.

2020-Q3.shortcut: Each person receives BOTH creams, one per arm, so the observations are naturally paired within a person. With a continuous response and normality, the paired t-test is the right procedure.
tips: Look for what shares a subject: two measurements on the SAME person are paired, and pairing must be preserved by analysing the within-person differences.
Pairing removes between-person variation, so the paired t-test is far more powerful here than the two-sample t-test, which wrongly treats the 2n measurements as independent.
The randomisation of which arm gets which cream protects against a left/right arm effect; it does not turn the design into an independent-samples one.
If normality could not be assumed, the correct non-parametric analogues would be the Wilcoxon signed-rank test or the sign test - both paired procedures, not the Mann-Whitney.
solution: Each of the n persons receives cream A on one arm and cream B on the other, so both treatments are observed on the same individual.
The two responses from one person are therefore dependent - a matched pair - and the natural analysis works with the n within-person differences d_i = A_i - B_i.
The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and the two-sample t-test both assume two INDEPENDENT samples, which is violated here.
A test for randomness addresses the order of a sequence and is irrelevant to comparing two treatments.
Given a continuous response and an assumption of normality for the differences, the appropriate procedure is the paired t-test on the d_i.
Hence option (c) is correct.

2020-Q4.shortcut: E(X) = n/(n-2) = 10/8 = 1.25 > 1, so statement 1 holds. Mode = [(m-2)/m][n/(n+2)] = (3/5)(10/12) = 0.5 < 1, so statement 2 fails.
tips: Two F formulas to memorise: mean = n/(n-2) using only the DENOMINATOR d.f., and mode = [(m-2)/m][n/(n+2)] using both.
The F distribution is positively skewed, so mode < median < mean. Since the mean is only 1.25, a mode below 1 is entirely expected - that intuition answers statement 2 before any arithmetic.
The mean of F(m,n) always exceeds 1 whenever n > 2, because n/(n-2) > 1. Statement 1 is therefore true for every admissible F distribution.
The mode is less than 1 for all m, n, since [(m-2)/m] < 1 and [n/(n+2)] < 1 - a general fact worth carrying.
solution: For X ~ F(m, n) with m = 5 and n = 10, the mean is E(X) = n/(n - 2), valid for n > 2.
E(X) = 10/(10 - 2) = 10/8 = 1.25, which is greater than 1. Statement 1 is TRUE.
The mode of F(m, n) for m > 2 is Mode = [(m - 2)/m] . [n/(n + 2)].
Since 0.5 < 1, statement 2 is FALSE.
Only statement 1 is correct, option (a).

2020-Q5.shortcut: A run is a maximal block of identical symbols. Count the changeovers: the sequence switches 21 times in 30 tosses, so there are 22 runs.
tips: Runs = number of changes of symbol + 1. Counting CHANGES is faster and far less error-prone than bracketing blocks.
Mark the sequence in groups as you read: H | TT | H | T | HHH | T | HH | TT | H | T | H | T | HH | T | H | TT | H | T | HH | T | H | T.

Sanity range: with 30 tosses the number of runs must lie between 2 and 30; a well-mixed fair sequence gives roughly n/2 + 1 = 16 or more, so 22 is plausible while 28 and 30 would be near-perfect alternation.
For the run test, the expected number of runs is 2 n1 n2/n + 1; here n1 = 16 heads and n2 = 14 tails give about 15.9, so 22 is on the high side, indicating more alternation than chance.
solution: A run is a maximal unbroken sequence of identical outcomes.
Reading the 30 tosses in order and grouping: H | TT | H | T | HHH | T | HH | TT | H | T | H | T | HH | T | H | TT | H | T | HH | T | H | T.
Counting the groups: 1 H, 2 TT, 3 H, 4 T, 5 HHH, 6 T, 7 HH, 8 TT, 9 H, 10 T, 11 H, 12 T, 13 HH, 14 T, 15 H, 16 TT, 17 H, 18 T, 19 HH, 20 T, 21 H, 22 T.
The group lengths sum to 1+2+1+1+3+1+2+2+1+1+1+1+2+1+1+2+1+1+2+1+1+1 = 30, confirming that every toss has been counted.
There are therefore 22 runs.
Option (b) is correct.

2020-Q6.shortcut: One sample, a hypothesised value for the location (250 hours), and no distributional assumption - that is exactly the one-sample SIGN test.
tips: Match the test to the design: ONE sample against a stated value = sign test (or Wilcoxon signed-rank); TWO independent samples = Mann-Whitney U or median test; fit to a distribution = K-S or chi-square.
The sign test simply counts how many of the 24 lifetimes exceed 250 and refers that count to a Binomial(24, 0.5) under H0 - no distributional assumption at all.
Mann-Whitney and the median test both need two samples, so options (b) and (c) are ruled out by the design alone.
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test would require a fully specified distribution, not just a claim about one quantile, so option (d) is also inapplicable.
solution: The manufacturer's claim concerns the location of a single population - that the lifetime typically exceeds 250 hours - and there is only one sample, of 24 observations.

The sign test is the standard one-sample non-parametric procedure for a hypothesised median or location value: count how many observations exceed 250 and compare that count with Binomial(n, 0.5) under H0.
The Mann-Whitney U test and the median test both compare TWO independent samples, so they do not apply.
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compares the empirical CDF with a fully specified theoretical distribution, which is not what is claimed here.
Hence the sign test is appropriate, option (a).

2020-Q7.shortcut: The probability integral transform makes F(X) ~ U(0,1). Since F is increasing, it preserves order, so F(X_(r)) is the rth order statistic of a U(0,1) sample.
tips: Probability integral transform: for continuous F, the variable U = F(X) is always Uniform(0,1), whatever the parent distribution. This is the single most useful transformation in order-statistic theory.
F is non-decreasing, so it maps the rth smallest X to the rth smallest U - order is preserved and the ranks carry over unchanged.
Consequence worth memorising: F(X_(r)) ~ Beta(r, n - r + 1), which gives E[F(X_(r))] = r/(n+1) - the basis of plotting positions in probability plots.
The result is distribution-free, which is exactly why non-parametric methods and simulation both rest on it.
solution: Let X have a continuous CDF F. The probability integral transform states that U = F(X) follows the Uniform(0,1) distribution.
Indeed, for 0 < u < 1, P(F(X) <= u) = P(X <= F^(-1)(u)) = F(F^(-1)(u)) = u, which is the U(0,1) CDF.
Applying F to each of X_1, ..., X_n gives a random sample U_1, ..., U_n from U(0,1).
Because F is non-decreasing, it preserves the ordering of the sample, so the rth smallest of the U values is F applied to the rth smallest X value: U_(r) = F(X_(r)).
Therefore F(X_(r)) is the rth order statistic of a sample of size n from the Uniform(0,1) distribution.
Option (b) is correct.

2020-Q8.shortcut: Substitute into r12.3 = (r12 - r13 r23)/sqrt((1-r13^2)(1-r23^2)). The numerator is sin^2 t - sin t cos t and the denominator is |sin t cos t|, so the ratio is tan t - 1.
tips: The denominator simplifies first: (1 - cos^2 t)(1 - sin^2 t) = sin^2 t cos^2 t, whose square root is |sin t cos t| - spotting this collapses the whole expression.
Factor the numerator as sin t (sin t - cos t) so that the common sin t cancels against the denominator, leaving (sin t - cos t)/cos t = tan t - 1.
Memorise the partial correlation formula r12.3 = (r12 - r13 r23)/sqrt((1 - r13^2)(1 - r23^2)); every item in this sub-topic is one substitution away from it.
Options (a), (b) and (d) all involve 2 theta, which never arises from this cancellation - a structural cue that (c) is the intended form.
solution: The partial correlation formula is r12.3 = (r12 - r13 r23)/sqrt[(1 - r13^2)(1 - r23^2)].
Substituting r12 = sin^2 t, r13 = cos t, r23 = sin t, the numerator is sin^2 t - (cos t)(sin t) = sin t (sin t - cos t).
For the denominator, 1 - r13^2 = 1 - cos^2 t = sin^2 t and 1 - r23^2 = 1 - sin^2 t = cos^2 t.
So the denominator is sqrt(sin^2 t cos^2 t) = |sin t cos t|.
Taking the principal branch where sin t cos t > 0, r12.3 = sin t (sin t - cos t)/(sin t cos t) = (sin t - cos t)/cos t.
This equals tan t - 1, option (c).

2020-Q9.shortcut: With only two individuals the second judge either agrees (d = 0, rho = 1) or reverses (sum d^2 = 2, rho = 1 - 12/6 = -1). No other outcome exists.
tips: Spearman's rho = 1 - 6 sum(d^2)/(n(n^2 - 1)). With n = 2 the denominator is 2(3) = 6, so rho = 1 - sum(d^2).
Only two rankings of two items are possible, so only two values of rho can occur - enumerate them rather than reasoning abstractly.
0 is impossible because sum(d^2) would have to be 1, but with n = 2 the differences are either both 0 or both +-1, giving sum(d^2) equal to 0 or 2.
General principle: for small n the set of attainable rank correlations is discrete, and the gaps between attainable values are large - a reason rank tests need adequate n.
solution: Spearman's rank correlation is rho = 1 - 6 sum(d_i^2)/(n(n^2 - 1)), where d_i are the differences of ranks.
There are only two possible rankings by the second judge. If the judges agree, the ranks are (1,2) and (1,2), so d = (0,0) and sum(d^2) = 0, giving rho = 1.
If the judges disagree, the ranks are (1,2) and (2,1), so d = (-1, +1) and sum(d^2) = 2, giving rho = 1 - 2 = -1.
No other configuration exists, so rho can only be -1 or +1; the value 0 is unattainable.
Option (b) is correct.

2020-Q10.shortcut: For n = 5 the median is the 3rd order statistic, so the constant is 5!/(2! 2!) = 30 and the density is 30 F^2 (1-F)^2 f.
tips: General order-statistic density: g_r(x) = [n!/((r-1)!(n-r)!)] [F(x)]^(r-1) [1 - F(x)]^(n-r) f(x). Substitute r and n and the whole answer follows.
For the median of 5 observations, r = 3, so the exponents are r - 1 = 2 and n - r = 2 - symmetric, as the median should be.
The constant 5!/(2!2!) = 120/4 = 30 is what separates (c) from (d); option (c) has the right shape but the wrong normalising constant.
Options (a) and (b) are the densities of the MAXIMUM and the MINIMUM respectively - useful to recognise as the r = n and r = 1 special cases.
solution: For a sample of size n from a continuous distribution, the density of the rth order statistic is g_r(x) = [n!/((r-1)!(n-r)!)] [F(x)]^(r-1) [1-F(x)]^(n-r) f(x).
With n = 5 observations, the sample median is the third order statistic, so r = 3.
The exponents are r - 1 = 2 on F(x) and n - r = 2 on 1 - F(x).
Hence the density of the sample median is 30 [F(x)]^2 [1 - F(x)]^2 f(x).
Option (d) is correct.

2020-Q11.shortcut: Statement 1 is imprecise: multiplying by a NEGATIVE constant multiplies the mean by it but multiplies the SD by its absolute value. Statements 2 and 3 state the rules correctly.
tips: Scaling rules: mean(cX) = c mean(X) but SD(cX) = |c| SD(X). The absolute value is compulsory because a standard deviation can never be negative.
Shift rules: mean(X + k) = mean(X) + k but SD(X + k) = SD(X). Dispersion is unaffected by a change of origin.
Statements 1 and 2 make claims about the same operation, and one is a corrected version of the other - a sure sign that the imprecise one is the false statement.
Variance scales as c^2: Var(cX) = c^2 Var(X). Taking the square root recovers |c|, which is where the absolute value comes from.
solution: Let Y = cX for a constant c. Then mean(Y) = c mean(X) and Var(Y) = c^2 Var(X), so SD(Y) = |c| SD(X).

Statement 1 asserts that both the mean AND the standard deviation are multiplied by the constant. This is true for the mean but false for the SD when c is negative, since a standard deviation is non-negative. FALSE as stated.
Statement 2 asserts that the SD is multiplied by the ABSOLUTE VALUE of the constant, which is exactly correct. TRUE.
Statement 3: for Y = X + k, Var(Y) = Var(X), so the SD is unchanged by a change of origin. TRUE.
Only statements 2 and 3 are correct.
Option (b) is correct.

2020-Q12.shortcut: Consistency requires every ultimate class frequency to be non-negative. Each of the three relations makes one such class negative - (AB) > (A) makes (A beta) < 0, (AB) < (A)+(B)-N makes (alpha beta) < 0, and the third makes (alpha beta gamma) < 0. All three signal inconsistency.
tips: Test for consistency by computing the ULTIMATE class frequencies; the data are inconsistent as soon as any of them is negative.
Two attributes give the standard bounds max(0, (A)+(B)-N) <= (AB) <= min((A),(B)). Statements 1 and 2 are simply violations of the upper and lower bound respectively.

For three attributes, inclusion-exclusion gives (alpha beta gamma) = N - (A) - (B) - (C) + (AB) + (AC) + (BC) - (ABC). Requiring this to be non-negative gives (ABC) <= (AB)+(AC)+(BC)-(A)-(B)-(C)+N; statement 3 is the violation of that bound.

When all listed relations are constructed as violations of the same non-negativity principle, expect 'all of them' - but derive at least the three-attribute one, since its sign is easy to get backwards.
solution: A set of attribute frequencies is CONSISTENT only if every ultimate class frequency is non-negative.
Statement 1: since the class AB is contained in A, we always have (AB) <= (A); indeed (A beta) = (A) - (AB) >= 0. So (AB) > (A) forces (A beta) < 0 and the data are inconsistent. CORRECT indicator.

Statement 2: (alpha beta) = N - (A) - (B) + (AB) must be non-negative, which gives (AB) >= (A) + (B) - N. So (AB) < (A) + (B) - N makes (alpha beta) < 0 and the data are inconsistent. CORRECT indicator.
Statement 3: by inclusion-exclusion, (alpha beta gamma) = N - (A) - (B) - (C) + (AB) + (AC) + (BC) - (ABC).

Non-negativity of (alpha beta gamma) requires (ABC) <= (AB) + (AC) + (BC) - (A) - (B) - (C) + N. Hence the strict inequality in statement 3 makes (alpha beta gamma) < 0 and signals inconsistency. CORRECT indicator.
All three relations indicate inconsistency, option (d).

2020-Q13.shortcut: In general Var(X - Y) = S_X^2 + S_Y^2 - 2 r S_X S_Y. The given identity removes the cross term, so 2 r S_X S_Y = 0 and hence r = 0.
tips: The variance of a difference carries a MINUS 2rS_X S_Y term; the plain additive formula holds only when that term vanishes.
Since standard deviations are strictly positive for non-degenerate variables, 2 r S_X S_Y = 0 forces r = 0 exactly - not merely 'small'.
Note this gives UNCORRELATED, not independent: the same identity would hold for dependent but uncorrelated variables.
Companion identity: Var(X + Y) = S_X^2 + S_Y^2 + 2 r S_X S_Y, which likewise reduces to the additive form precisely when r = 0.
solution: For D = X - Y, the general variance formula is S_D^2 = S_X^2 + S_Y^2 - 2 r S_X S_Y, where r is the correlation between X and Y.
The question states that S_D^2 = S_X^2 + S_Y^2.
Equating the two expressions gives S_X^2 + S_Y^2 - 2 r S_X S_Y = S_X^2 + S_Y^2.
Hence 2 r S_X S_Y = 0.
Since S_X and S_Y are positive for non-degenerate variables, r = 0.
Hence the correlation is exactly zero, option (c).

2020-Q14.shortcut: Y = 20 - X makes X + Y = 20 identically, so (X + Y)X = 20X. The correlation of X with 20X is +1.
tips: Simplify the expression BEFORE computing anything: the sum X + Y collapses to the constant 20, which is the entire content of the question.
Correlation between a variable and a positive multiple of itself is exactly +1; a negative multiple would give -1.
The variance sigma^2 is stated only to guarantee that X is non-degenerate so that the correlation is defined - it never enters the answer.
Option (a) -1 is the correlation between X and Y themselves, the natural trap if you stop at Y = 20 - X without simplifying the product.
solution: Since Y = 20 - X, the sum X + Y = X + (20 - X) = 20 is a constant.
Therefore the second variable is (X + Y)X = 20X.
The correlation between X and 20X is Cov(X, 20X)/(sd(X) . sd(20X)) = 20 Var(X)/(sd(X) . 20 sd(X)) = 1.
In general, corr(X, aX) equals +1 for a > 0, and here a = 20 > 0.
The finite variance sigma^2 > 0 ensures the correlation is well defined.
Hence the correlation is 1, option (d).

2020-Q15.shortcut: r^2 = 0.49 gives 49% explained variation, so statement 1 holds. Since r = +0.7 > 0, both regression coefficients share that positive sign, so statement 2 holds and statement 3 fails.
tips: Percentage of variation explained is r^2 x 100, not r x 100. Here 0.7^2 = 0.49, i.e. 49%.
Sign rule: r, b_yx and b_xy always carry the SAME sign, because r^2 = b_yx b_xy and r = sign(b) sqrt(b_yx b_xy).
Statements 2 and 3 are direct contradictions, so exactly one of them must be true - decide by the sign of r and both are settled at once.
Remember 'r^2 explains, r describes': r^2 is the coefficient of determination and r merely indicates strength and direction.
solution: The correlation coefficient is r = 0.7.
Statement 1: the proportion of variation in the dependent variable explained by the independent variable is the coefficient of determination r^2 = 0.49, i.e. 49%. TRUE.
The two regression coefficients satisfy b_yx b_xy = r^2 and both carry the same sign as r.
Statement 2: since r = +0.7 is positive, both regression coefficients are positive. TRUE.
Statement 3: this contradicts statement 2 and is therefore FALSE.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct, option (b).

2020-Q16.shortcut: R^2 = (r12^2 + r13^2 - 2 r12 r13 r23)/(1 - r23^2) = 2rho^2(1-rho)/[(1-rho)(1+rho)] = 2rho^2/(1+rho). Taking the square root gives sqrt(2) rho/sqrt(1+rho).
tips: Compute R SQUARED first and take the square root only at the very end - working with R directly invites algebraic slips.
The cancellation of (1 - rho) between numerator and denominator is the whole trick; factor 1 - rho^2 as (1-rho)(1+rho) before simplifying.
Check the limit rho -> 1: R^2 -> 2/2 = 1, so R -> 1 as the variables become perfectly correlated. Option (d) satisfies this; option (a) gives 1/sqrt2 and fails.
This is the square root of the 2018 Q29 result - the same identity appears in both papers, once as R^2 and once as R.
solution: For a trivariate distribution, R^2_(1.23) = (r12^2 + r13^2 - 2 r12 r13 r23)/(1 - r23^2).
With r12 = r13 = r23 = rho, the numerator is rho^2 + rho^2 - 2rho^3 = 2rho^2(1 - rho).
The denominator is 1 - rho^2 = (1 - rho)(1 + rho).
Cancelling (1 - rho), which is non-zero since rho is not 1, gives R^2_(1.23) = 2rho^2/(1 + rho).
Taking the positive square root: R_(1.23) = sqrt(2) rho/sqrt(1 + rho).
Hence option (d) is correct.

2020-Q17.shortcut: X - Y and X + Y are independent N(0,2) variables (their covariance is Var(X) - Var(Y) = 0). So U is the ratio of two independent chi-square(1)/1 quantities, i.e. F(1,1).
tips: For i.i.d. normals, the sum and the difference are INDEPENDENT - a special property of the normal family that this question is built on.
Cov(X - Y, X + Y) = Var(X) - Var(Y) = 0, and joint normality then upgrades zero correlation to full independence.
The common variance 2 cancels in the ratio, so no scaling constant survives - the answer is a pure F with 1 and 1 degrees of freedom.
Equivalently (X-Y)/(X+Y) is a standard Cauchy, and the square of a Cauchy is F(1,1). Both routes give option (d).
solution: X and Y are independent N(0,1), so X - Y ~ N(0,2) and X + Y ~ N(0,2).
Cov(X - Y, X + Y) = Var(X) - Var(Y) = 1 - 1 = 0, and since the pair is jointly normal, X - Y and X + Y are INDEPENDENT.
Set A = (X - Y)/sqrt(2) and B = (X + Y)/sqrt(2); these are independent N(0,1).
Then U = ((X-Y)/(X+Y))^2 = A^2/B^2, and A^2 and B^2 are independent chi-square variables each with 1 degree of freedom.
By definition, the ratio (chi-square_1/1)/(chi-square_1/1) of independent chi-squares follows F(1, 1).
Hence U ~ F(1,1), option (d).

2020-Q18.shortcut: Each sample variance loses one degree of freedom for its estimated mean, so the d.f. are 20 - 1 = 19 and 37 - 1 = 36.
tips: Rule: the variance-ratio F test uses (n1 - 1, n2 - 1) degrees of freedom when both population means are UNKNOWN and estimated from the samples.
If the means were KNOWN, no degree of freedom would be lost and the d.f. would be n1 and n2 - the reason the question specifies 'unknown means'.
Order matters only for reading the table: place the larger variance in the numerator so that F >= 1, then use the corresponding d.f. first.
Option (a) subtracts 2 from each sample size, confusing this with the pooled t-test's n1 + n2 - 2 - keep the two adjustments apart.
solution: To test the equality of two normal variances we use the ratio of the two sample variances, F = s1^2/s2^2.
Each sample variance is computed about its own SAMPLE mean, because the population means are unknown, so one degree of freedom is lost per sample.
For the first sample of size 20, the numerator d.f. is 20 - 1 = 19.
For the second sample of size 37, the denominator d.f. is 37 - 1 = 36.
Hence the statistic follows F(19, 36) under the null hypothesis.
Option (b) is correct.

2020-Q19.shortcut: Under H0 the count of observations above 25 is Binomial(10, 0.6). The size is P(X >= 7) = 0.2150 + 0.1209 + 0.0403 + 0.0060 = 0.382.
tips: The size of a test is the rejection probability computed UNDER H0, so use p = 0.6 (the null quantile), not 0.5.
Sum all four upper terms: P(7), P(8), P(9) and P(10). Stopping at P(X = 7) = 0.215 gives a badly understated size.
Since the mean of Binomial(10, 0.6) is 6, a cut-off of 7 is barely above the mean, so a LARGE size is expected - options (a), (b) and (c) are implausibly small.
solution: Under H0 the upper 60th percentile equals 25, so P(X > 25) = 0.6 and the number of observations exceeding 25 in a sample of 10 is Binomial(10, 0.6).
The test rejects H0 when this count is at least 7, so the size is P(B >= 7) with B ~ Binomial(10, 0.6).
The size of the test is approximately 0.38, option (d).

2020-Q20.shortcut: The winner has the MINIMUM time. For U(a,b) with n observations, E[min] = a + (b-a)/(n+1) = 10 + 1/11.
tips: Uniform order-statistic means: E[X_(r)] = a + (b - a) r/(n+1). For the minimum r = 1 and for the maximum r = n - two formulas in one.
The winner is the FASTEST, i.e. the smallest time, so r = 1. Reading 'winner' as the maximum gives 10 + 10/11 and no matching option.
The n + 1 in the denominator is the standard 'plotting position' divisor - the n order statistics divide the interval into n + 1 equal expected gaps.
With 10 runners on a 1-second interval, the expected winning margin below 10 seconds is 1/11 = 0.0909 s - a small, plausible figure.
solution: The ten finishing times are i.i.d. Uniform(10, 11), and the winner's time is the minimum, X_(1).
For a sample of size n from U(a, b), the rth order statistic has mean E[X_(r)] = a + (b - a) r/(n + 1).
For the minimum, r = 1, so E[X_(1)] = a + (b - a)/(n + 1).
Substituting a = 10, b = 11 and n = 10: E[X_(1)] = 10 + 1/11.
Numerically this is 10.0909 seconds.
Hence the expected time of the winner is 10 + 1/11, option (a).
